questiontext.text: Which best describes the core mechanism of binary search?

answer.text: Compare the target with the middle element and discard the half that cannot contain it, repeatedly halving the interval

feedback.text: Correct — each comparison halves the remaining search space.

answer.text: Scan every element in order from the start

feedback.text: That is linear search.

answer.text: Estimate the probe position from the target's value

feedback.text: That is interpolation search.

answer.text: Split the interval using Fibonacci numbers

feedback.text: That is Fibonacci search.

generalfeedback.text: Binary search repeatedly compares the middle element and eliminates half of the remaining range.

questiontext.text: What is the worst-case time complexity of binary search over n elements?

answer.text: O(log n)

feedback.text: Correct — halving the range gives about log₂ n steps.

answer.text: O(n)

feedback.text: That is linear search; binary search halves each step.
Only the best case (target at the middle) is constant.

answer.text: O(n log n)

feedback.text: Too large; a single search is logarithmic.

generalfeedback.text: Each step discards half the elements, so at most ~log₂ n comparisons are needed.

questiontext.text: What precondition must the input array satisfy for binary search to be correct?

answer.text: It must be sorted

feedback.text: Correct — binary search relies on order to decide which half to keep.

answer.text: It must be unsorted

feedback.text: No — without order the halving logic breaks.

answer.text: Its values must be uniformly distributed

feedback.text: Uniform distribution helps interpolation search, not binary search.

answer.text: It must contain only distinct values

feedback.text: No — binary search works with duplicates too.

generalfeedback.text: Binary search requires a sorted array (and random access) so it can rule out half the range at each comparison.

questiontext.text: Why is binary search a poor fit for a singly linked list?

answer.text: A linked list lacks O(1) random access, so reaching the middle element is itself O(n)

feedback.text: Correct — jumping to the midpoint costs O(n), defeating the speedup.

answer.text: Linked lists cannot store sorted data

feedback.text: No — a linked list can certainly be kept in sorted order.

answer.text: Binary search only works on floating-point values

feedback.text: No — it works on any ordered keys.

answer.text: Linked lists use too much memory

feedback.text: Not the reason; the issue is indexing cost.

generalfeedback.text: Binary search needs O(1) indexing to reach the midpoint; a linked list only offers sequential access.

questiontext.text: Which statements about binary search are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It runs in O(log n) time in the worst case

feedback.text: Yes — the range halves each step.

answer.text: It requires the array to be sorted

feedback.text: Yes — order is what lets it discard half the range.

answer.text: It works correctly on unsorted arrays

feedback.text: No — it requires sorted input.

answer.text: It runs in O(n) time in the worst case

feedback.text: No — that is linear search; binary search is O(log n).

generalfeedback.text: Binary search: O(log n) worst case, requires sorted input and random access.

questiontext.text: Binary search returns correct results on an unsorted array.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — without a sorted order the discarded half may contain the target.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — binary search requires the array to be sorted.

questiontext.text: Iterative binary search uses only O(1) extra (auxiliary) space.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — it keeps just a few index variables.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: The iterative version needs only constant extra space.
